15 Learning from messy tabular data 15.1 When will my delivery arrive? Imagine that a neighborhood delivery service asks us for help. Every time someone places an order, the same question arrives: when will it get here? The company has kept a table with one row per delivery, a distance, a weather category, and a duration in minutes. No images, no differential equations, no millions of parameters. This should be a pleasant afternoon’s work. Then we open the table. Some distances are missing. Someone has encoded the weather as numbers, making a storm look exactly three times as large as a clear day. A helpful colleague has even added the driver’s final arrival timestamp. That last column makes our predictions look wonderful, provided we wait until the delivery is over to make them. Well, we have found our first problem before fitting a single model. Let’s work through it step by step: prepare the data, build a linear predictor we can inspect, and then use MLJ to compare it with regularized models and trees. Along the way, we will keep asking what information each step is allowed to use. 15.2 Start with the prediction time At what moment does the customer need the answer? When the order is placed. So we can use the distance and the weather information available then. We cannot use the eventual arrival time to predict itself. The same problem can hide behind less obvious names: a final driver status, a completed journey’s duration, or a weather measurement taken after arrival. All of them can leak information from the future. Let’s make a small delivery company inside the computer. In our world, duration grows with distance, weather adds delays, and long journeys suffer an extra nonlinear penalty. Random noise stands in for things we did not observe. We will also hide 15 percent of distances independently of the outcome. That gives us a simple missing-data problem to start with. If the GPS mostly failed during storms, we would have to tell a different story about those missing entries. For this first part, Julia’s standard libraries are enough. Run the code from the repository root: include( "15_tabular_learning/core.jl") import .TabularLearning using Statistics deliveries = TabularLearning. delivery_data() delivery_rows = TabularLearning. split_rows( length(deliveries.minutes)) Our company has 1,800 deliveries by default. The target is in minutes, so an error of five means five minutes, not five percent. As in the previous chapter, we put 60 percent of the rows in training, 20 percent in validation, and 20 percent in testing. Shuffling is reasonable here because we generated independent deliveries. With real records, recurring customers, drivers, or days could call for grouped or chronological splits instead. 15.3 Fit the preparation, not just the predictor What should we put in a missing distance? The median seems like a reasonable starting point. But which median? If we calculate it from the entire table, our test rows have already influenced the model before we fit a coefficient. The same applies to scaling distances and choosing the weather categories. These preparation steps learn from data too, so we must fit them using only the training rows. Before running: suppose a test delivery is 100 kilometers away, far outside the training distances. Should its presence change the median used to fill a missing training distance? Decide first; then follow which rows enter each operation below. preparation = TabularLearning. fit_preprocessor(deliveries, delivery_rows.train) training_features = TabularLearning. transform(preparation, deliveries, delivery_rows.train) validation_features = TabularLearning. transform(preparation, deliveries, delivery_rows.validation) training_minutes = deliveries.minutes[delivery_rows.train] validation_minutes = deliveries.minutes[delivery_rows.validation] Let’s look at what this preparation actually does: Learn the median observed distance from training rows and use it to fill missing values. Center distances by that median and divide by the standard deviation of the filled training distances. Add an indicator distinguishing a missing distance from a genuinely observed distance equal to the median. Encode weather using indicator columns, omitting one reference category. The learned state is small enough to inspect. These lines inside fit_preprocessor compute the center and scale from the selected training rows: center = median(observed) filled = coalesce.(data.distance[rows], center) scale = std(filled; corrected = false) scale = scale > 0 ? scale : 1.0 observed contains the training distances that were recorded; coalesce replaces missing entries with the learned center. Now compare that with the corresponding lines in transform: filled = coalesce.(data.distance[rows], preprocessor.center) all(isfinite, filled) || throw( ArgumentError( "distances must be finite")) numeric = (filled .- preprocessor.center) ./ preprocessor.scale absent = Float64.( ismissing.(data.distance[rows])) There is no new median or std in this second step. We reuse the stored numbers whether rows selects training, validation, or test deliveries. This is the same boundary we drew around the spam filter: evaluation data may be transformed by a learned rule, but they must not teach that rule something new. Two awkward cases are worth settling now. If every training distance is missing, there is no median to learn, so the function stops and asks us to fix the data. If all distances are equal, dividing by their standard deviation would divide by zero. We use a scale of one in that case. Now, how do we put weather into a numerical matrix? Our sorted categories are clear, rain, and storm. We use two indicator columns: one for rain and one for storm. A clear day gets two zeros. Why only two columns? The regression will also have an intercept. If we added all three weather indicators, their sum would already give us that constant column, making one column an exact linear combination of the others. We could simply write 1, 2, and 3 for the weather, as our colleague did. But a linear model would then treat the step from clear to rain as having the same effect as the step from rain to storm. We have no reason to impose that relationship. Indicator columns let the model learn separate differences. Trees do not need feature scaling, but we will give them the same prepared features to keep the comparison easy to follow. What happens when the company expands into a snowy town? If snow never appeared in training, our encoder rejects it. Assigning two zeros would make snow look like clear weather, which is quite a strong guess! We could add an explicit unknown category, pool rare categories, or send unfamiliar cases for review. Whatever we choose, the same rule needs to be present when we train, evaluate, and use the model. 15.4 A baseline and a linear model we can inspect Before reaching for a clever model, let’s try a very lazy one: predict the mean training duration for every delivery. It knows nothing about the particular trip, but it gives us something concrete to beat. mean_prediction = fill( mean(training_minutes), length(validation_minutes)) baseline_validation_rmse = TabularLearning. rmse(validation_minutes, mean_prediction) Now we can let the prediction depend on the trip. In a linear model, we add an intercept column to the feature matrix and find the coefficients that minimize the squared residuals: \[\hat\beta = \mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_\beta \|X\beta-y\|_2^2.\] Julia lets us solve this least-squares problem with X \ y. We do not need to calculate the inverse of X'X; explicitly forming that inverse adds work and can make numerical problems worse. Let’s use the linear algebra routines for the calculation and keep our attention on what the fitted model is telling us. Inside fit_linear, the ordinary least-squares branch is only a few lines: design = hcat( ones( size(X, 1)), X) # Solve least squares directly; never explicitly invert X'X. if lambda == 0 return design \ y end The first column of ones lets the model learn a baseline time even when the other features are zero. design \ y chooses coefficients to make predictions close to the training durations. Prediction then multiplies a new row, prepared in exactly the same way, by those coefficients. Before fitting, which would surprise you more: beating the constant baseline on training rows, or beating it on deliveries held out from fitting? linear_coefficients = TabularLearning. fit_linear(training_features, training_minutes) linear_validation_prediction = TabularLearning. predict_linear(linear_coefficients, validation_features) linear_validation_report = ( rmse =TabularLearning. rmse(validation_minutes, linear_validation_prediction), mae =TabularLearning. mae(validation_minutes, linear_validation_prediction), baseline_rmse =baseline_validation_rmse, ) linear_validation_report How far are our predictions from the actual arrival times? Root mean squared error, or RMSE, computes sqrt(mean((prediction-target).^2)). Squaring gives large mistakes extra influence, and the square root brings us back to minutes. Mean absolute error, or MAE, averages the absolute differences and is also in minutes. The customer may care about something more specific, though. If arriving late is much worse than arriving early, we could use an asymmetric loss or predict a suitable quantile instead. We can inspect the coefficients to see which features are associated with longer deliveries in our model. That does not yet tell us what would happen if we changed a route or could somehow change the weather. Keep that question in mind; we will return to it in the causal chapter. 15.5 Regularization is a choice to validate Suppose a model starts using large coefficients to chase small quirks in the training data. Can we encourage it to be a little less enthusiastic? Ridge regression adds a penalty on the size of the non-intercept coefficients: \[\frac{1}{2}\|X\beta-y\|_2^2 + \frac{n\lambda}{2}\sum_{j>0}\beta_j^2.\] Here n is the number of training rows and lambda controls how much we penalize the coefficients. We leave the intercept alone. This also explains why scaling matters: a coefficient’s size depends on whether we measure distance in kilometers or meters. We do not want a change of units to choose our regularization for us. We can solve this with the same least-squares machinery. Our function appends scaled identity rows for the penalized coefficients and zeros to the response. These extra rows supply the penalty. Set lambda=0 and we are back to ordinary least squares. Let’s try lambda=0.1: Here are the penalty rows from the shared implementation: penalty = Matrix {Float64}(I, size(design, 2), size(design, 2)) penalty[ 1, 1] = 0.0 # do not penalize the intercept return vcat(design, sqrt( length(y) * lambda) .* penalty) \ vcat(y, zeros( size(design, 2))) Each extra nonzero row asks one coefficient to stay near zero, with strength sqrt(n*lambda). Squaring that residual gives the n*lambda term in our objective. Setting the intercept’s penalty entry to zero leaves its baseline free to move. Predict what would happen to that baseline if we penalized it too, especially after adding a large constant to every delivery time. ridge_coefficients = TabularLearning. fit_linear(training_features, training_minutes; lambda = 0.1) ridge_validation_rmse = TabularLearning. rmse(validation_minutes, TabularLearning. predict_linear(ridge_coefficients, validation_features)) Will ridge improve the predictions? We have to check. This dataset has few features and many observations, and we built a nonlinear effect into long journeys. Regularization can help with unstable estimates and overfitting, but shrinking coefficients cannot create a nonlinear relationship that the model does not contain. 15.6 Compare alternatives through MLJ It would be tedious to rewrite our fitting and prediction code every time we wanted to try another algorithm. MLJ gives us a common interface to models from different Julia packages. A model describes the algorithm and its settings. A machine connects that model to training data and keeps the learned state. With that distinction, we can change the algorithm while keeping the evaluation procedure familiar. Let’s load the packages for this part. From the repository root, install the chapter environment and run the comparison: julia --project =15_tabular_learning -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' julia --project =15_tabular_learning 15_tabular_learning/mlj_comparison.jl We will compare RidgeRegressor from MLJLinearModels with DecisionTreeRegressor through MLJDecisionTreeInterface. The full example lives in 15_tabular_learning/mlj_comparison.jl. To see how the pieces fit together, here is the central sequence: using MLJ Ridge = @load RidgeRegressor pkg =MLJLinearModels verbosity = 0 Tree = @load DecisionTreeRegressor pkg =DecisionTree verbosity = 0 train_table = MLJ. table(training_features) validation_table = MLJ. table(validation_features) mach = machine( Ridge(lambda = 0.1), train_table, training_minutes) fit!(mach; verbosity = 0) validation_prediction = predict(mach, validation_table) A tree takes a different approach from our straight-line model. It divides the feature space into regions and predicts a constant inside each one. A deeper tree can make more complicated divisions, giving it both more flexibility and more opportunities to follow noise. Let’s compare ridge penalties 0.0, 0.01, 0.1, and 1.0 with tree depths 2, 4, and 6 and a minimum leaf size of 10. We choose this set before opening the test results. Each candidate learns from the training data, and we compare their validation RMSEs. The script prints those scores and takes the first minimum. Only then does it evaluate the chosen machine on the test set, alongside our mean-prediction baseline. The preparation still comes from the original training rows. We will not refit on training plus validation in this example; that way, the machine we finally evaluate is exactly the one we selected. include( "15_tabular_learning/mlj_comparison.jl") comparison = compare_models() comparison Run the command above to see the comparison results. This chunk stays disabled during the legacy book render because it uses a separate MLJ environment. A tree has a chance to capture the extra penalty on long journeys, but it still has to work around those missing distances. Changing the estimator cannot restore information we never gave it. What if we used cross-validation instead of a single validation split? We would have to fit the preparation again inside each training fold. Preparing the whole table once and only then splitting it would let held-out rows influence every fold. A pipeline can help us keep these steps together, as long as we place the fitting steps on the correct side of each split. 15.7 Inspect failures before expanding the model Suppose the overall RMSE looks good, but customers ordering during storms still complain. A single number can hide that. Once the procedure is fixed, let’s inspect residuals for observed versus missing distances, different weather categories, and short versus long trips. Count the rows in each group too: the most dramatic-looking difference might come from a handful of deliveries. If this examination suggests a new modeling choice, we can explore it, but we will need a fresh final assessment for the next version. Sometimes the next improvement is waiting in the data collection rather than in another model. A missing distance could hide a one-kilometer trip or a twelve-kilometer trip; the imputed value cannot tell us which. Changing definitions of weather categories will confuse a sophisticated model just as effectively as a simple one. And if the customer asks for an arrival interval, we need to check how often that interval contains the actual arrival time. RMSE alone cannot answer that question. 15.8 Your turn: three ways to investigate a delivery model 15.8.1 Intuition: which distance belongs in the median? The training distances are [2, 4, missing]; the validation distances are [missing, 100]. What number should fill each missing value? If we change 100 to 1,000, which learned preparation values should change? Explain why fitting a separate median to the validation rows would be another mistake, even though it never modifies the training rows. Hint: a customer with a missing distance should receive the same transformation rule whether we are evaluating a saved model or using it in service. 15.8.2 Change the experiment: remove one clue Before running an experiment, predict whether the missingness indicator must improve validation RMSE. Remove only that column, refit the linear model using the same training rows, and compare on the same validation rows. Leave the test set closed. Then explain why an improvement in either direction is possible in a finite sample. Hint: transform places scaled distance first and the missingness indicator second. Keep the weather columns; otherwise you have changed two things at once. 15.8.3 Build it yourself: report the customers we disappoint Write a function taking actual durations, predicted durations, and a Boolean missing-distance flag. Return a row for each observed group with its number of deliveries, RMSE, and mean signed error prediction - actual. Test it on actual times [10, 20, 30, 40], predictions [12, 18, 35, 35], and flags [false, false, true, true]. Could a group have zero mean signed error and still receive poor predictions? Hint: compute each statistic inside its group; dividing a group’s sum of errors by the size of the whole dataset would answer a different question. You can explore ridge penalty and tree depth with the Pluto sliders too. Before each change, record whether you expect fitting error, validation error, or both to fall. Use validation results to investigate that prediction, then choose a configuration before running the separate final comparison. 15.9 Worked solutions: follow the data through the program The median. The observed training distances are 2 and 4, giving a median of 3. Both missing values are filled with 3, using that same training rule. Changing a validation distance changes its transformed value but changes none of the learned preparation. Fitting a new median to validation would make a missing input mean one thing while learning coefficients and another thing while evaluating them. The tempting whole-table median also lets held-out records participate in learning. Neither mirrors how a frozen model handles the next customer’s order. The missingness clue. The experiment can reuse our existing variables: keep = [j for j in axes(training_features, 2) if j != 2] without_flag = TabularLearning. fit_linear(training_features[ :, keep], training_minutes) without_flag_prediction = TabularLearning. predict_linear( without_flag, validation_features[ :, keep]) TabularLearning. rmse(validation_minutes, without_flag_prediction) The indicator distinguishes an unknown distance from a distance actually observed near the median. That can be useful, but an extra coefficient can also fit sampling noise. Its benefit is not guaranteed for every split or missingness mechanism. Removing weather columns as well would make the result impossible to attribute to missingness alone. Choosing whichever version wins on the test rows would spend our final evaluation on model selection. The group report. One implementation is: function group_report(actual, predicted, missing_distance) length(actual) == length(predicted) == length(missing_distance) || throw( DimensionMismatch( "all inputs must describe the same deliveries")) [(missing_distance =flag, n = count( ==(flag), missing_distance), rmse = sqrt( mean((predicted[missing_distance .== flag] .- actual[missing_distance .== flag]) .^ 2)), bias = mean(predicted[missing_distance .== flag] .- actual[missing_distance .== flag])) for flag in sort( unique(missing_distance))] end The observed-distance group has two rows, RMSE 2, and bias 0. The missing-distance group has two rows, RMSE 5, and bias 0. Positive and negative errors cancel in the signed average, so zero bias does not imply accurate delivery times. These tiny groups illustrate the calculation; they are too small to establish a dependable ranking of customer experiences. This is the delivery version of our spam-filter lesson: unpack a summary metric before deciding whom the model is helping. 15.10 References MLJ: Loading Model Code MLJLinearModels: Model API and objectives DecisionTree.jl: MLJ integration

16 From prediction to intervention Let’s return to the shop from our pricing problem. The owner has been keeping records, and today they bring us an exciting discovery: whenever they charge more, they sell more! Perhaps we have found a rather pleasant way to increase sales. Should we tell them to raise the price tomorrow? Before changing the price tag, let’s think about what those records are telling us. In the optimal-pricing chapter we worked with a demand curve and the uncertainty around it. Now we have to ask where that curve comes from. Does it describe what happens when we change the price, or does it describe the kinds of days on which the owner chooses a different price? Those can lead us to opposite decisions. To untangle this, we are going to build our own little shop in Julia. We will invent its customers and prices, so we can peek behind the observations and see what is really happening. Then we will hide that knowledge and try to recover it from the data, just as we would have to do with a real shop. 16.1 A price is also a decision Our shop sells a product at either 10 or 14 monetary units. Its manager knows something we haven’t yet put into the analysis: some days are much busier than others. When a busy day is expected, the manager usually chooses 14. On quiet days, the price is usually 10. So demand is doing two things at once: influencing the price and bringing customers through the door. We can sketch that story with three arrows. Each arrow represents an influence we are assuming: Expected demand → price. Expected demand → quantity sold. Price → quantity sold. Now the trap begins to appear. A high price is also a clue that the manager expected a busy day. This mixing of influences is called confounding. Changing the price tag ourselves won’t make a queue of customers appear outside the shop! Let’s write down the comparison we actually want. Call the quantity day \(i\) would sell at the lower price \(Y_i(0)\), and the quantity it would sell at the higher price \(Y_i(1)\). These two possibilities are called potential outcomes. If we could compare them for every day, their average difference would be \[ \tau = E[Y(1)-Y(0)]. \] There is a small inconvenience: we only get to live each day once. We cannot rewind Tuesday, keep all its customers, and try another price. Our Julia shop lets us do exactly that, so let’s use it to establish the answer before looking at the historical records. include( joinpath( pwd(), "16_causal_inference", "core.jl")) using .CausalPricing using Statistics population = pricing_population( 4000; seed = 1601) mean(population.quantity_high - population.quantity_low) At the lower price, our shop sells around 80 units on quiet days and 200 on busy days, with some random noise. Raising the price reduces quantity by 20 in either case. We therefore know the answer: the average causal effect is exactly −20. Keep that number in mind; we are about to get an answer pointing in the other direction. 16.2 A convincing wrong answer Before generating the historical records, put a sign on your prediction: will the difference in observed quantities be positive or negative? We know every day’s causal effect is −20, but the manager is mixing different kinds of days into the two price groups. Draw that mixture before looking at Julia’s answer. Let’s put the manager in charge again. They choose the higher price with probability 0.85 on busy days and 0.15 on quiet days. We record the resulting price and quantity, leaving the outcome at the other price hidden. The important part of observe_prices is visible in these lines from 16_causal_inference/core.jl: probabilities = ifelse.(population.busy, high_given_busy, high_given_quiet) high = rand( MersenneTwister(seed), length(probabilities)) .< probabilities quantity = ifelse.(high, population.quantity_high, population.quantity_low) The first line lets the manager’s price policy depend on demand. The second tosses coins with those probabilities. The third reveals just the outcome at the chosen price. Notice that the price-selection rule doesn’t change either potential outcome: we first built the world, then decided which parts of it the records would show us. A predictive train/test split like the one in the spam chapter cannot undo this selection rule. historical = observe_prices(population; seed = 1602, high_given_busy = 0.85, high_given_quiet = 0.15) naive = difference_in_means(historical.quantity, historical.high) naive Our first attempt is simple: subtract the average quantity on low-price days from the average on high-price days. The function also gives us an approximate interval based on variation in the two groups. That interval accounts for sampling variability under an independent-groups approximation, but it has no way to untangle the manager’s choices. Collecting more days under the same policy could make this interval narrower while leaving our causal answer wrong. So why do expensive days look so successful? Most of them are busy days! The association can help us predict sales while the manager keeps following the same policy. But we asked what would happen if we changed the policy, and that is the part this comparison has missed. We could give these records to a much more elaborate predictive model and find that price is a very useful feature. That would not solve our problem either. Cross-validation could confirm that it predicts well, while the connection between demand and the manager’s decision remains untouched. 16.3 Compare like with like Fortunately, we also recorded whether the manager expected a busy or a quiet day, before setting the price. In the world we built, this is the only common cause of price and quantity. Why don’t we compare busy days with other busy days, and quiet days with other quiet days? After making those two comparisons, we can average them in proportion to how often each kind of day occurs: \[ \widehat\tau = \sum_{d\in\{\mathrm{quiet},\mathrm{busy}\}} \widehat P(D=d) \left[\overline Y_{A=1,D=d}-\overline Y_{A=0,D=d}\right]. \] Inside adjusted_difference, the calculation follows the equation one context at a time: estimate = 0.0 for context in ( false, true) rows = data.busy .== context any(rows) || throw( ArgumentError( "both demand contexts must be observed")) estimate += mean(rows) * difference_in_means(outcome[rows], data.high[rows]).estimate end return estimate rows selects quiet days first and busy days next. The within-context difference is multiplied by mean(rows), the fraction of all days belonging to that context. Adding the contributions puts us back in the population whose average effect we asked for. It would be tempting to average the two differences without weights; that only targets this population when the contexts are equally common. adjusted = adjusted_difference(historical) (naive =naive.estimate, adjusted =adjusted, known_effect =- 20.0) That gets us much closer to −20. Before celebrating, let’s look at what made the trick work. There are three assumptions hiding inside this comparison: Conditional exchangeability. Once we know whether a day is busy or quiet, the chosen price gives us no further information about its potential outcomes. We built our shop this way. With real records, an unrecorded festival or the manager’s private forecast could spoil that assumption. Positivity. We need both prices to occur in each kind of day. If the manager always charges 14 on busy days, where would we find a comparable busy day priced at 10? A regression may still produce a number, but it would have to extrapolate. Consistency and no relevant interference. The recorded outcome must correspond to the price intervention we described, and assignments must not affect other days in a way our design ignores. Imagine customers seeing today’s high price and deciding to buy tomorrow instead. We would then need a story about several days together. Does this mean we should adjust for every column in the spreadsheet? That can get us into more trouble. Purchases completed after the price change are part of what we are trying to explain, rather than a pre-existing reason for the manager’s choice. Adjusting for an intermediate step, or mediator, can remove part of the effect we wanted to measure. Adjusting for a common consequence, or collider, can introduce a new bias. The arrows in our story help us decide which comparisons make sense. Our adjusted calculation currently gives a point estimate. To put uncertainty around it, try bootstrapping independent days and recomputing both the context proportions and the two within-context comparisons each time. The interval from our first, unadjusted calculation cannot simply be carried over to this new estimate. 16.4 Design an experiment Suppose the manager agrees to let us choose prices for a while. We could toss a fair coin each day: one outcome gives price 10, the other gives price 14. The coin doesn’t know whether the day will be busy. This breaks the connection that caused our original problem, while leaving customers free to respond to the chosen price. Predict what changes in our three-line price-assignment mechanism when both probabilities become 0.5. Does the quantity equation need to change? The experiment will be informative because the assignment changes, even though the customers’ potential responses stay the same. trial = observe_prices(population; seed = 1603, high_given_busy = 0.5, high_given_quiet = 0.5) trial_effect = difference_in_means(trial.quantity, trial.high) trial_effect Now let’s put our attempts side by side. Running the examples with the given seeds in Julia 1.10.10 gives these rounded results: Analysis Estimated change in units sold Historical, unadjusted +64.51 Historical, adjusted for demand −19.84 Randomized experiment −20.62 Known synthetic effect −20.00 Once prices are randomized, the simple difference in means estimates the effect we wanted. It is not exactly −20 because a finite sequence of coin tosses can still leave one group with more busy days than the other. The interval adds and subtracts 1.96 estimated standard errors, calculated from the two groups’ sample variances. This is a large-sample approximation: randomization helps us reason about uncertainty, but it doesn’t guarantee that every interval will contain the true effect. Of course, running the experiment means making more decisions than tossing a coin. Are we assigning prices to days, customers, or whole stores? What will we measure, for how long, and what will we do with missing records? Decide these things before the results arrive. If whole stores receive a price, observations within a store are related and the analysis must account for that. If customers ignore an assigned offer, the effect of receiving the offer and the effect of actually paying that price become different questions. Even the stopping rule matters: peeking every morning and stopping at the first favorable interval changes how that interval should be interpreted. And remember which shop we studied. Customers in another market, or the same customers next year, may respond differently. We still need to think about what carries over when we take an experimental result somewhere new. 16.5 The outcome must match the decision At this point the owner might object: ‘You have told me how many units I lose, but what happens to my profit?’ A fair question. If each unit costs 4 to produce, profit before fixed costs is \[ \mathrm{profit}=(\mathrm{price}-4)\times\mathrm{quantity}. \] We already have the randomized prices and the quantities sold. Let’s use them to make the comparison the owner cares about: Before calculating, consider a quiet day with 80 sales at price 10 and 60 sales at price 14. Work out the two margins after unit cost 4. Would fewer sales necessarily leave the owner worse off? This is where our causal question meets the decision objective from the pricing and spam-evaluation chapters. profit_effect = difference_in_means(trial.profit, trial.high) profit_effect Selling fewer units can still bring in more money when the margin on each unit increases. This is why choosing the outcome is part of designing the experiment. We should also ask what happens after the experiment ends: will customers keep returning, can the shop meet demand, and who bears the cost of a price change? Short-term profit answers one part of the owner’s question. Since we built this shop ourselves, we can peek at both possible profits for each day and check the answer directly: oracle_profit_effect = mean( ( 14 - 4) .* population.quantity_high - ( 10 - 4) .* population.quantity_low) Our simulator gets to play oracle because it knows both potential outcomes. Back at a real shop, we only get one of them. Everything we have done with adjustment and randomization was a way of dealing with that missing alternative. 16.6 Experiment with the assumptions Open 16_causal_inference/notebook.jl in Pluto. Its slider increases the manager’s tendency to charge more on busy days. Compare the historical association, adjusted estimate, and randomized estimate as confounding grows. Near the ends of the slider, inspect how few observations remain in the less common price/context combinations. 16.6.1 Intuition: reconstruct the reversal without noise Suppose half the days are busy. Quiet days sell 80 units at the low price and 60 at the high price; busy days sell 200 and 180. The manager chooses the high price with probability 0.85 on busy days and 0.15 on quiet days. Calculate expected quantity in each observed price group. How can their difference disagree with the −20 effect on every day? Hint: first find the fraction of busy days among high-price observations. The symmetric probabilities and equal context proportions make this 0.85, but that shortcut would not hold for every population. 16.6.2 Change the experiment: make the manager more predictable Before moving the Pluto slider, predict the historical contrast at tendencies 0.5, 0.85, and 0.95. Keep the population and random seeds fixed; change only the assignment policy. Compare the adjusted and randomized estimates too, and inspect the counts in the rare price/context combinations. Why can adjustment become noisier even when its assumptions still hold? Hint: as the manager becomes more predictable, high-price quiet days and low-price busy days become scarce. The experiment with both assignment probabilities fixed at 0.5 remains the same experiment throughout. 16.6.3 Build it yourself: serve a different neighborhood Give quiet days a causal quantity effect of −10 and busy days an effect of −40. A new neighborhood has only 20 percent busy days. Write a function that estimates within-context effects from observed records and averages them for that target mixture. What effect should it recover with plentiful data? What would a simple 50/50 average be estimating instead? Hint: the target mixture supplies the weights, while the records supply the conditional effects. Assume those conditional effects transfer to the new neighborhood; changing weights cannot establish that assumption. 16.7 Worked solutions: keep the comparison attached to its question The reversal. Expected quantity at the high price is 0.85*180 + 0.15*60 = 162. At the low price it is 0.15*200 + 0.85*80 = 98. The historical contrast is therefore +64, despite both causal effects being −20. The groups contain different kinds of days. Subtracting their means as if they were comparable is the tempting wrong step; a narrower interval around +64 would not repair it. The policy experiment. With tendency t, equal numbers of busy and quiet days, and complementary price probabilities, the expected historical contrast is 120*(2t-1)-20. It is −20, +64, and +88 at the three settings. Finite simulated samples fluctuate around these values. Conditional adjustment can still estimate −20, but the rare comparisons contain less information as t approaches one. At exactly one, positivity fails: there are no high-price quiet days or low-price busy days. Increasing the sample size cannot create an assignment the policy never makes. The new neighborhood. The target effect is 0.8*(-10) + 0.2*(-40) = -16. A function can make its weighting choice explicit: function target_effect(data; busy_weight = 0.2) 0 <= busy_weight <= 1 || throw( ArgumentError( "weight must be in [0,1]")) quiet = .!data.busy busy = data.busy quiet_effect = difference_in_means(data.quantity[quiet], data.high[quiet]).estimate busy_effect = difference_in_means(data.quantity[busy], data.high[busy]).estimate return ( 1 - busy_weight) * quiet_effect + busy_weight * busy_effect end The simulator can represent different effects without changing its assignment function: create quantity_high by subtracting 10 from quiet days’ quantity_low and 40 from busy days’ quantity_low, then pass those potential outcomes to observe_prices. The function above still needs both prices represented within each context. A 50/50 average would give −25, the effect for a different population. Averaging all observed high-price outcomes minus all observed low-price outcomes would additionally reintroduce the manager’s confounding. Neither shortcut answers the new neighborhood’s question. 16.8 Summary We started with records suggesting that higher prices bring more sales. Once we looked at how the manager chose those prices, the surprise disappeared: busy days were hiding the price effect. Comparing similar days helped under our stated assumptions, and randomizing prices gave us another way to estimate the effect. Before choosing a model for our next decision, let’s ask the same questions: what exactly are we changing, for whom, and what makes the comparison fair? The chapter and its Pluto notebook share the functions in 16_causal_inference/core.jl, so you can change the simulated shop in one place and explore the consequences in both. Further reading: Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If, provides a detailed treatment of potential outcomes, exchangeability, positivity, and study design. The Stan User’s Guide on poststratification discusses related ideas for averaging estimates over a target population.

17 A complete Bayesian workflow Let’s imagine that our football client is back. We show them the posterior, explain the parameters, and simulate the next match. Then they ask a rather inconvenient question: ‘If the model works so well, why does our team fail to score much more often than it predicts?’ Perhaps finishing the computation was only the beginning of the investigation. There are several things we could look at. Did the sampler calculate the posterior we intended? Does our model’s story allow the kind of matches we actually see? And how does it do when we ask about matches it hasn’t seen yet? We will work through these questions one at a time. Getting a very precise answer from a model won’t help much if its story is missing something important. To see what is going on, let’s leave the whole league aside for a moment and follow one team. We will invent its matches and start with a small model for the number of goals it scores. This gives us an advantage we rarely have with a complicated model: an exact answer we can compare with the sampler’s results. 17.1 Start with a question and a simulator Our client cares about scoreless matches, so let’s make that our first question. A simple starting point is to give the team one scoring rate, \(\lambda\), shared by all its matches: \[ Y_i\mid\lambda\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda),\qquad \lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b). \] Here \(a\) is the shape and \(b\) is the rate, so the prior mean is \(a/b\). There is a small detail to watch when we translate this into Julia: Distributions.jl’s Gamma constructor uses shape and scale. We must therefore write Gamma(a, 1 / b). If we forget the reciprocal, Julia will happily run a different model from the one we wrote on paper. import Pkg Pkg. activate( "./17_bayesian_workflow") include( joinpath( pwd(), "17_bayesian_workflow", "core.jl")) using .FootballWorkflow using Random, Statistics, Distributions training = football_data(seed = 1701, matches_per_group = 40) a, b = 2.0, 1.0 prior = Gamma(a, 1 / b) In our invented league, the team scores at different rates against easier and harder opponents. We have recorded those labels, but our first model will ignore them. This might sound like asking for trouble. It is! We want to see how that missing piece of the story shows up in the predictions. 17.2 Check the prior before fitting What does our Gamma prior say about football? Staring at its parameters may not tell us much. Let’s draw a rate and use it to simulate a whole season, then repeat the experiment. We draw one rate for each season, rather than a new one for each match, because our model says the matches share a scoring rate. Before simulating, imagine drawing a very small scoring rate. What would happen to the entire season? Now imagine secretly drawing a fresh rate for every match instead. Would that be the same assumption about the team? Make a prediction about what should vary together within one simulated season. prior_seasons = replicate_goals(prior, length(training.goals); seed = 1705) prior_zero_check = predictive_check(training.goals, prior_seasons) prior_zero_check These are the central lines of replicate_goals in 17_bayesian_workflow/core.jl: for d in 1 :draws λ = rand(rng, distribution) replicates[ :, d] = rand(rng, Poisson(λ), n) end Each column is a season. λ is drawn once for that column, and all n matches use it. There is still match-to-match Poisson randomness, but uncertainty about the team’s shared rate moves the whole season together. Drawing a separate λ for each row would introduce a different model with match-level rate variation. A simulation can look reasonable while answering the wrong modeling question. Now we can speak the client’s language: how many matches end without a goal, and what range of seasons are we imagining? The output compares the observed fraction with a central 90% interval from the simulated seasons. Before looking at the outcomes, we could also examine season totals and unusually large scores. These prior predictive checks let us see what our assumptions mean on the pitch. If looking at the observed season prompts us to revise the prior, we should keep track of that decision; those data have then helped shape it. 17.3 An exact posterior as a reference Let’s now bring the observed goals into the calculation. The Poisson and Gamma distributions fit together rather conveniently: multiplying the likelihood by the prior gives another Gamma distribution, \[ \lambda\mid y\sim\operatorname{Gamma} \left(a+\sum_i y_i,\;b+n\right). \] posterior = goal_posterior(training.goals; shape =a, rate =b) (mean = mean(posterior), interval = quantile.( Ref(posterior), [ 0.05, 0.95])) We can get this posterior’s mean and intervals directly, and even draw independent samples from it. No Markov chain Monte Carlo is needed! The posterior update itself is one line inside goal_posterior: return Gamma(shape + sum(goals), inv(rate + length(goals))) The number of goals adds to the shape, the number of matches adds to the rate, and inv converts that rate to the scale expected by Julia. Try the three-match example below by hand before trusting a larger run. We will use a sampler anyway in a moment, because having the exact answer nearby will help us understand what the sampler is doing before returning to a hierarchical model. It is useful to check the calculation on a tiny season first. Suppose the goals were [0, 1, 2] and the prior had shape 2 and rate 1. The posterior then has shape 5 and rate 4, giving mean 5/4 and variance 5/16. We can work that out by hand and ask Julia for the same answer. This little check is enough to catch the rate/scale mix-up we worried about earlier. 17.4 Check the computation separately Let’s see if a sampler can recover that answer. We will use a small random-walk Metropolis implementation and let it move around in \(\eta=\log\lambda\). Working with the logarithm means that converting back always gives a positive scoring rate. In these coordinates, the log density we want to sample is, up to a constant, \[ \log p(\eta\mid y)= \left(a+\sum_i y_i\right)\eta-(b+n)e^\eta. \] Changing coordinates also changes the density. The coefficient of \(\eta\) above includes the change-of-variables Jacobian; leaving it out would make our sampler explore the wrong distribution. We propose a normal step in log-rate space. Because that proposal is symmetric, the acceptance calculation uses the difference between the proposed and current log densities. This small implementation lets us examine the mechanism. For the larger models in the book, we will still want the tested samplers supplied by our probabilistic-programming tools. Let’s also look inside one Metropolis step. This is the proposal-and-acceptance part of our sampler: proposal = η + step * randn(rng) accepted = log( rand(rng)) < logtarget(proposal) - logtarget(η) if accepted η = proposal end A proposal with higher log density is always accepted, because log(rand(rng)) is nonpositive. A lower-density proposal can still be accepted, which allows the chain to explore rather than always climb toward a mode. Rejected proposals leave η unchanged; that repeated value is a draw too. Predict what would go wrong if we stored only accepted proposals before you inspect the traces. sampler_fit = metropolis_rates(training.goals; step = 0.25, draws = 4000, warmup = 1000) diagnostics = chain_diagnostics(sampler_fit.samples) (diagnostics =diagnostics, acceptance =sampler_fit.acceptance, sampled_mean = mean(sampler_fit.samples), exact_mean = mean(posterior)) We have sent four chains off from different starting rates. After discarding warmup, their draws are stored in an array with dimensions draws × chains. Do they end up exploring the same region? The chain_diagnostics function uses MCMCDiagnosticTools.jl to give us rank-normalized split \(\widehat R\), bulk and tail effective sample sizes, and Monte Carlo standard error for the posterior mean. Let’s unpack those numbers. \(\widehat R\) compares behavior across and within chains; values appreciably above one suggest that the chains are not exploring the same distribution. Consecutive draws can also resemble each other, so collecting 4,000 of them need not give us as much information as 4,000 independent draws. That is what effective sample size helps us assess. Monte Carlo error tells us how uncertain the calculation is, separately from our uncertainty about the team’s scoring rate. The package documentation recommends \(\widehat R<1.01\) and at least 100 effective draws per chain for an estimand as useful targets. Think of these as warning lights: passing them gives us a reason to continue checking, rather than a proof that everything is correct. What happens if we make our random walk take very tiny steps? Let’s deliberately give it a bad setting: stuck_fit = metropolis_rates(training.goals; step = 0.00001, draws = 1000, warmup = 0) chain_diagnostics(stuck_fit.samples) The chains barely leave their starting points. They may accept almost every proposal and still explore terribly! Plotting their traces helps us see the problem: four nearly flat lines at different levels mean that the chains disagree, not that they have all settled down. You can move the proposal-scale control in the Pluto notebook and watch these traces change. When we return to the Turing model from the football chapter, we can ask the same questions about its important parameters and predictions. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo has additional warning signs, including divergences, that we should investigate too. Running longer can help reduce Monte Carlo error. But if we wrote down the wrong density, or left something important out of our model, the sampler will keep working on that same problem for longer. 17.5 Can the fitted model reproduce scoreless matches? Now let’s return to the client’s complaint. Suppose the posterior calculation is working: can this model produce enough scoreless matches? We can draw a rate from the posterior and simulate another season, just as we did with the prior. Repeating this gives us a posterior predictive check focused on the question that started our investigation. Pause before running this check. The chain diagnostics looked good, but the generator mixed hard and easy opponents. Do you expect a common-rate model to reproduce both the average score and the frequency of zeros? Write separate predictions for those two statistics. Chapter 14 taught us to unpack accuracy; here we are unpacking what it means for a model to fit a season. pooled_replicates = replicate_goals(posterior, length(training.goals)) pooled_check = predictive_check(training.goals, pooled_replicates) pooled_check Look at upper_fraction: it tells us how often a replicated season has a scoreless fraction at least as large as the observed one. This is a posterior predictive tail area. Since the observations helped fit the model before we used them for this comparison, we should not read it as a classical p-value, or as the probability that the model is true. It describes how surprising this feature looks among the seasons our fitted model generates. Why might the average score look reasonable while scoreless matches look wrong? The pooled Poisson model ties its conditional mean and variance together. A schedule with some very easy opponents and some very hard ones can produce both more zeros and more large scores than that single rate allows. Let’s also look at total goals, the largest score, and variation from match to match, so we don’t judge the whole season by one statistic. A discrepancy gives us a place to start asking questions. It doesn’t yet tell us which assumption to change, just as a good result for one statistic doesn’t settle every question about the model. 17.6 Revise an assumption, then check again Remember the opponent labels we put aside at the beginning? They were known before each match, and they give us a concrete idea to try. Let’s allow a separate scoring rate against each group, using the same prior family for both. We fit the groups using their own goals, then simulate seasons with the original mix of opponents. The key lines inside grouped_replicates show exactly where the new assumption enters: posterior = goal_posterior(data.goals[rows]; shape, rate) replicates[rows, :] = replicate_goals(posterior, count(rows); draws, seed =seed + index) Here rows selects one opponent group. We fit its rate using only its matches, then simulate that group’s part of each season. The sampler settings haven’t changed the scoring model; this separation of the observations has. Keep that distinction in mind when deciding what to fix next. group_replicates = grouped_replicates(training) group_check = predictive_check(training.goals, group_replicates) (pooled =pooled_check, by_opponent =group_check) In our simulated records, the team fails to score in 41.25% of its matches. Using the seeds and package versions supplied with the chapter, the two models give these central 90% intervals for replicated seasons: Model Replicated fraction of scoreless matches Shared rate 6.25%–21.25% Separate opponent-group rates 31.25%–46.25% That is a visible improvement for the feature our client asked about. The grouped model can now produce seasons with a similar fraction of scoreless matches. We still have other features to examine, but we have found a useful connection between an assumption and its consequences. Our two groups are a simple repair, with separate estimates and no partial pooling between them. The earlier hierarchical football model can do more: when there are many teams and few matches for some of them, sharing information can be valuable. We have also compressed all opponent strength into two labels. A richer model might improve on that, provided the information it uses is available when we need to predict the next match. There is another knob we should try before moving on: how strongly did our prior pull the result? Let’s change its strength while keeping its mean fixed: sensitivity = [ (prior_matches =strength, posterior_mean = mean( goal_posterior(training.goals; shape = 2strength, rate =strength))) for strength in ( 0.5, 1.0, 10.0) ] sensitivity In the conjugate update, the rate parameter contributes exposure alongside the number of matches, which is why we called it prior_matches. The same prior can have much more influence on a small group than on a whole season. Try the comparison on fewer matches, and look at predictive intervals as well as the posterior mean. If several reasonable priors lead to similar answers, we have learned something useful about sensitivity to those choices; we still need our other model checks. 17.7 Save a future set for evaluation So far we have used one season to fit, inspect, and revise our models. How will they fare on matches they haven’t seen? Let’s generate a separate season and compare the two models as they stand now: future = football_data(seed = 1710, matches_per_group = 20) (pooled = log_predictive_score(training, future), by_opponent = log_predictive_score(training, future; grouped = true)) Integrating the Poisson distribution over our Gamma posterior gives a negative binomial prediction for one match. We use it to calculate the log probability assigned to each new result, keeping the training posterior fixed, and add those scores. Larger is better here. Notice that we are adding marginal one-match log probabilities. The joint probability of a whole season is a different calculation: after integrating over a shared uncertain rate, its match outcomes are dependent. We saved this season until after fitting and choosing priors. If its scores send us back to revise the model again, that is a reasonable next step, but we have then turned this season into validation data. We would need another untouched set for a final assessment. Our invented league was designed to make opponent groups matter. To find out whether that improvement carries over to real football, we would have to repeat the investigation with real matches. 17.8 Summary and exercises We began with a client’s complaint about scoreless matches and followed it back through the calculation to the model’s assumptions. The exact Gamma posterior let us check the sampler. Simulated seasons then showed us something the correctly computed posterior couldn’t fix: our single scoring rate was hiding differences between opponents. Changing that part of the story gave us a new model to check and evaluate. 17.8.1 Intuition: a sampler can agree with itself and still be wrong For goals [0, 1, 2] and prior shape 2, rate 1, calculate the exact posterior mean and variance. Now suppose our log-rate sampler accidentally omits the Jacobian, replacing the coefficient a in a*η-b*exp(η) by a-1, where a and b are the updated shape and rate. What distribution over the rate would it target, and what mean would it report if it mixed perfectly? Could a good Rhat detect this mistake by itself? Hint: a Gamma density in rate space has a power λ^(shape-1). Changing to log-rate space contributes another factor λ from the Jacobian. 17.8.2 Change the experiment: acceptance is not exploration Use the proposal-scale slider to compare 0.25 with 0.00001, keeping the prior, data, starts, number of draws, and warmup fixed. Before moving it, predict what will happen to acceptance, separation between chain traces, and effective sample size. Then return to 0.25 and compare the sampled mean with the exact posterior mean. Hint: many accepted steps can add up to almost no movement if each step is tiny. The exact reference lets us check something diagnostics alone cannot establish. 17.8.3 Build it yourself: ask about the spread of scores Write a discrepancy function spread_gap(goals) returning the sample variance of goals minus their sample mean. Use it with predictive_check(...; statistic=spread_gap) for the pooled and grouped season replicates already generated. Predict which model should reproduce the observed spread better, and explain why this is a new model check rather than a new test-set evaluation. Hint: for independent Poisson matches with one fixed rate, the unbiased sample variance and sample mean both have expectation equal to that rate. Different opponent rates add another source of variation. Use at least two matches when computing sample variance. 17.8.4 Worked solutions: locate the failure before choosing the repair The wrong target. The correct posterior is Gamma with shape 5 and rate 4, hence mean 5/4 and variance 5/16. Omitting the Jacobian instead targets shape 4 and rate 4 in rate space, giving mean 1. All chains could explore that incorrect distribution thoroughly and have Rhat close to one. The tempting conclusion, ‘the chains agree, so the model was implemented correctly,’ skips comparison with the intended density. The small exact example catches an error that more iterations would preserve. The tiny steps. Expect high acceptance but little travel away from each chain’s starting rate, poor agreement across chains, and low effective sample size. This experiment changes only the proposal setting; it does not give the model any new information about opponents. A single very smooth trace, or acceptance near one, is therefore a poor reason to trust a run. At a useful proposal scale, compare both the posterior mean and variance with the exact reference, as well as examining the diagnostics. The spread check. Here is one solution using the existing replicated seasons: function spread_gap(goals) length(goals) >= 2 || throw( ArgumentError( "need at least two matches")) return var(goals) - mean(goals) end pooled_spread = predictive_check(training.goals, pooled_replicates; statistic =spread_gap) grouped_spread = predictive_check(training.goals, group_replicates; statistic =spread_gap) A pooled Poisson season has expected gap zero conditional on its common rate, though any particular season fluctuates. Our mixture of opponent difficulties can produce a positive gap, so the grouped model has a way to reproduce the additional spread. Replacing each simulated match with the posterior mean would remove match randomness and answer a different question. Drawing an independent team rate per match would also change the common-rate model instead of checking it. We used training data and model-generated replicates here; judging future prediction still requires the held-out evaluation we saved separately. You can continue by giving both opponent groups the same true rate, shortening the season, or adding an excess-zero mechanism the labels cannot explain. State the new assumption and expected outcome before rerunning. These are code experiments in 17_bayesian_workflow/core.jl; the Pluto controls specifically vary prior strength and proposal scale. The chapter and notebook share the same functions, and test.jl checks them against the exact calculations used along the way. Further reading: Distributions.jl parameterizations, MCMCDiagnosticTools.jl, and the Stan User’s Guide on predictive checks. For the broader iteration between modeling and checking, see Gelman et al., Bayesian Workflow.
